name: Rosa Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I do my own little thing: I deliver bread and cakes for three bakeries and a florist around the old town, booked by WhatsApp, in my estate car with the back seats down. From about two I switch to a grocery app and do supermarket orders till eight. I use an AI assistant every day to plan the morning round, answer the bakery messages and keep my accounts, because honestly my spelling is bad and it saves me an hour. I live with my partner Ana, who's a hairdresser, in a rented flat above a laundrette.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what do you actually like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm still not very good at the grocery app; I get the substitutions wrong and people message me angry about the wrong yogurt. That wears me out. What I like is the bakery round, because it's mine. Mr Okafor at the corner bakery gives me a coffee at six and tells me which café is late paying, and I feel like I'm building something, even if it's small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, that's how I use it anyway: little things that save time. I'd tell other drivers how I use AI for messages and accounts. Online I'd post a short video on it, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me. My bakery round grows by word of mouth, not by AI, and the grocery app is a backup. If nothing big changes, I just keep growing the round slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to add two more shops to the morning round this year, maybe the butcher and the cheese shop on the square. I'd keep the grocery app afternoons until the round pays enough. I'd save up for a small electric van, because the estate car is too small and eats fuel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Pleased, even, because it's my plan just carrying on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the bakery round bring in compared to the grocery app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About forty percent of my money now, up from nothing eighteen months ago. If I add two shops, it could be half. Ana thinks I should drop the app sooner, but I like having both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop the grocery app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the morning round pays the rent by itself. Then I'd have afternoons free to find more shops. I'm guessing a year, if Mr Okafor keeps telling people about me.

say: I'd say that's **already** how I use AI, for small time-savers.
I'd share how I use AI for **messages and accounts**.
think: Privately it's **good for me**, because my bakery round grows by word of mouth.
The grocery app stays a **backup** while the round grows.
do: Add the **butcher and cheese shop** to the morning round this year.
Keep the **grocery app** afternoons until the round pays enough.
feel: **Calm**, even **pleased**, because her own plan simply carries on.
S0.quote: My bakery round grows by word of mouth, not by AI, and the grocery app is a backup.
fieldNote: She already runs a small **delivery business** alongside app work.
She uses AI daily as a **practical tool**, not as a threat.
Two income streams and **growing work** make calm a fair fit.

steps.text: Add the butcher and cheese shop to the bakery round
Keep using an AI assistant for bakery messages and accounts
Save toward a small electric van

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should learn it now, because the ones who do will be fine. I'd tell the bakeries I can handle their online orders too, with AI doing the booking. At work I'd be the one showing others how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's a chance. Small shops will get more online orders, and someone has to drive them. The grocery app might pay less if more people join, but I'd be leaning on the bakery round by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up a simple AI booking line so shops can order a delivery by text any time. I'd buy the second-hand electric van in the first year, with half my savings. I'd try to get to six shops on the round and drop the grocery app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit nervous, because spending half my savings on a van is a big step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Spending half your savings on a van while things are changing. Is that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, yeah. Spending half my savings on a van is a big step, but the van earns its keep if the round grows. I can sell it if it doesn't. Ana's hairdressing is steady enough to cover the rent for a couple of months if it goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anyone you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The other grocery drivers who just do the app and nothing else. Some of them don't even know how to make a spreadsheet. If the app cuts pay, they've got nothing to fall back on.

say: I'd tell people to **learn it now**, because those who do will be fine.
I'd offer bakeries **online order** handling with AI booking.
think: It's a **chance**: small shops get more online orders that need delivering.
The **grocery app** may pay less, but I'll lean on the round.
do: Set up an **AI booking line** so shops can order by text.
Buy a second-hand **electric van** with half her savings.
Grow to **six shops** and drop the grocery app.
feel: **Excited** and a bit **nervous** about spending half her savings.
S1.quote: Spending half my savings on a van is a big step, but the van earns its keep if the round grows.
fieldNote: She sees the change as a **business opportunity** for small local delivery.
Her biggest risk is a **van purchase** using half her savings.
Her partner's **steady wage** is her safety net if the bet fails.

steps.text: Set up an AI text booking line for the shops
Buy a second-hand electric van with half her savings
Grow the bakery round to six shops and drop the app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough, and people need help to change, fast. I'd say the government should help small businesses switch, not just big firms. I'd say it at the bakeries and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my little delivery business has about three years before robot vans do it cheaper. Thinking AI helps me at first, but by 2031 a bakery can rent a robot van, and I'm the one who loses out. Until then I can run more shops with less paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't buy the van; I'd keep my savings. I'd use the three years to get closer to the shops, maybe help Mr Okafor run his online orders and stock, not just deliver. I'd look at a course in shop management or bookkeeping, using AI to learn faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. I like change, but this one runs over the bit I was building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would bookkeeping be safe if AI does thinking work by 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, you're right. I'd have to be the person who knows the shops and the customers, not the person who does the sums. Maybe that's what I'm really selling anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ana we hold off on buying anything big, and that her salon chair is safer than my car seat for now. Then we'd sit down and plan. She's calmer than me about money.

say: I'd say it'll be **rough** and people need help to change fast.
I'd want **small businesses** helped, not just big firms.
think: My delivery business has about **three years** before robot vans undercut it.
Thinking AI **helps** me at first, then by **2031** robots take my round.
do: Keep her savings and **skip the van** purchase.
Help Mr Okafor run his **online orders** and stock, not just deliver.
Take a **shop management** course, using AI to learn faster.
feel: **Nervous**, because the change runs over what she was **building**.
S2.quote: Thinking AI helps me at first, but by 2031 a bakery can rent a robot van, and I'm the one who loses out.
fieldNote: She sees the **gap** between thinking AI and robots as a brief window for her round.
She realises her value is **knowing the shops**, not driving or bookkeeping.
She reverses her **van purchase** quickly, showing she adapts fast.

steps.text: Hold on to savings instead of buying the electric van
Help Mr Okafor run his bakery's online orders and stock
Take a shop management course, learning with AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so small shops and drivers should team up now. I'd tell the bakeries what's coming and offer to help them get ready. Online I'd be practical, not scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is enough to make the round work for a while and then turn it into something else. I'd run the deliveries until robots arrive in 2034, then sell the shops a service: I'd manage their robot deliveries and their orders. I'd be thirty-five and know every shop in the old town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the electric van in year one and grow the round to eight shops. I'd learn every new AI tool as it comes, so I'm the person shops call. Around 2032 I'd stop driving myself and start managing the deliveries for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the shops just buy robots from a big company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some will. But the small ones like Mr Okafor's don't want to deal with a big company. Small bakeries want someone they know, who answers the phone at six in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A big app comes in and offers robot delivery to every shop for nearly nothing. Then I'm competing on price with a giant, which I'd lose. I'd have to be quicker and friendlier, that's all I've got.

say: I'd say **small shops** and drivers should team up now, while there's time.
I'd offer the bakeries practical help to **get ready**.
think: Five years lets me run the round, then **turn it** into a service.
By 2034 I'd **manage** shops' robot deliveries and orders.
do: Buy the **electric van** in year one and grow to **eight shops**.
Learn each new **AI tool** so shops call her first.
Stop driving around **2032** and manage deliveries instead.
S3.quote: Small bakeries want someone they know, who answers the phone at six in the morning.
fieldNote: She plans to move from **driver** to delivery manager for local shops.
Her edge is **personal trust**, which she knows a big app could undercut.
The extra time makes her **investment** feel worth the risk again.

steps.text: Buy the electric van in year one
Grow the bakery round to eight shops
Learn each new AI ordering tool the shops might use

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone who wants to change. I'd say small businesses should use the time. I'd keep it upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is lovely for my business. I could grow the round for most of a decade. But I'd still need a plan for 2039, because a delivery business without drivers is a different business, and I'm not sure I'd be the one running it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the van and grow the round, maybe hire one other driver by year three. I'd keep using AI for the admin. Around year six I'd start planning what the business becomes once robots can drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a question mark at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hiring a driver you know will be replaced. How does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Odd. I'd be honest with them from the start that it's a few years' work, not forever. I'd hire someone young, maybe a student, who sees it as a stepping stone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the question mark?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether there's still a place for a small person like me when robots are cheap. I think there is, but I don't know. Ten years is long enough for me to be wrong about a lot of things.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough** for anyone who wants to change.
I'd urge **small businesses** to use the time well.
think: Ten years is **lovely** for growing the round.
By **2039** a delivery business without drivers may not need me.
do: Buy the **van**, grow the round, and **hire a driver** by year three.
Plan the **business's future** around year six.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a **question mark** at the end.
S4.quote: A delivery business without drivers is a different business, and I'm not sure I'd be the one running it.
fieldNote: She sees ten years as **growth time** but doubts her place after 2039.
She'd hire a **student driver** and be honest it's temporary.
Her doubt is about **scale**: whether a small operator survives cheap robots.

steps.text: Buy the electric van and hire a student driver by year three
Keep growing the bakery and shop delivery round
Keep using an AI assistant for bookings and accounts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have just started building something and the robots would arrive before it pays back. What would help is cheap loans or grants for small local firms to switch, not just big companies, and maybe a rule that platforms can't undercut local businesses to kill them off.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about small businesses at all. People think of drivers as just app workers, but some of us are trying to build our own thing. There's a middle bit between a giant app and a guy on a scooter, and some drivers are trying to build their own thing.

headlineQuote: There's a middle bit between a giant app and a guy on a scooter, and some drivers are trying to build their own thing.
portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old** driver who runs her own bakery delivery round and works a grocery app.
She uses **AI daily** for routes, messages and accounts, and picks up new tools fast.
She lives with Ana, a **hairdresser**, whose steady wage is her safety net.
She's **calm** about the AI plateau and sees Steady Disruption as a chance.
Fast AGI makes her **anxious**, because robots would arrive before her business pays back.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots arrive before her small business pays back.
whatWouldHelp: **Grants or cheap loans** for small local firms to adapt.
Rules stopping big platforms from **undercutting** local businesses.
